challenges.name: exports-imports-quiz
challenges.title: What can another module inject?
challenges.description: Three pieces of evidence from the CodeDev API: a chain of module imports, a quick fix for a missing CourseService, and a progress service that remembers the current user.

questions.explanation: False. Imports are not transitive: a module sees only the exports of the modules it imports itself. CourseModule exports CourseService but not UserModule, so EnrollmentModule gets CourseService and nothing else. Startup fails with: Nest can't resolve dependencies of the EnrollmentService (CourseService, ?). Please make sure that the argument UserService at index [1] is available in the EnrollmentModule context. The fix is to add UserModule to EnrollmentModule's imports, which also documents the dependency. Re-exporting UserModule from CourseModule would work too, but then every importer of CourseModule silently depends on users. The misconception is that the module graph shares everything along a path, the way JavaScript imports load everything they touch.

False. A class listed in the providers of two modules becomes two providers: Nest creates one CourseService for CourseModule and another for EnrollmentModule, each with its own cache. PATCH /courses/42 goes through CourseController and invalidates the cache of CourseModule's instance only; EnrollmentService keeps quoting from its own instance's stale outline for up to 10 minutes. The right fix is imports: [CourseModule] in EnrollmentModule (CourseModule already exports CourseService), which gives EnrollmentService the same instance that CourseController uses. The misconception is that a provider is a single global object no matter where it is declared: sharing comes from exporting and importing, not from naming the class twice.

True. Without a scope option, a provider is a singleton: one ProgressService for the whole application. Request 1 sets currentUserId to u_12 and waits about 25 ms for the outline; 3 ms later request 2 sets the same field to u_95; when request 1 resumes, it reads u_95, which is exactly what the log shows. The fix is to keep per-request data out of singleton fields: complete(userId, lessonId) with the controller passing req.user.id. Scope.REQUEST would also stop the mix-up, but it creates a new service, controller and dependency chain for every request, so it is the expensive answer to a problem an argument solves. The misconception is that each HTTP request gets its own service objects by default.
